lines: Last time, we ended on a simple observation: a commit protocol only matters because of the operations that actually produce commits.
So today we look at Delta's own DML, starting with the operation that does the most work by far — MERGE.
Here's the setup. A MERGE statement matches eleven rows out of a thousand sitting in one file.
With deletion vectors turned off, how much of that file do you think actually gets rewritten — just those eleven rows, or the whole thing?
answer: The whole file. Delta tables work by rewriting whole data files, not individual rows inside them.
So MERGE has to locate the file by its row range, then rewrite every single row in it, whether that row matched the condition or not.

lines: And that's exactly what happens here, for real: rewriting a thousand-row file to change eleven of them costs about seventeen and a half kilobytes written.
Nothing about that file's contents mattered for finding it — only which row IDs it was known to contain.
Turn deletion vectors on, and the picture changes completely. The old file is never touched.
Instead, a real bitmap marks the old versions of the matched rows as gone, and a tiny new file holds only the rows that actually changed — roughly seventy times less data written for the same update.
Now a trickier case. A MERGE reads the table and plans to rewrite file one. Before it can commit, a concurrent compaction job finishes first and removes that exact file.
Does the MERGE's commit just go through anyway, fail outright, or get some kind of chance to recover?
answer: It gets a chance to recover — but only after a real conflict. MERGE and compaction are explicitly allowed to collide under Delta's own rules.
So the commit is rejected, not silently accepted and not silently dropped.

lines: That's the real shape of it: the conflict fires because the file MERGE planned to touch is exactly the file compaction just removed — the precise pair Delta's documentation calls out by name.
From there, the MERGE simply re-reads the current state, finds the compacted replacement, reapplies the same condition, and commits cleanly on the next attempt.
Here's where row identity gets interesting. Take one specific row, then rewrite it into a brand new file at a brand new position.

Its materialized ID — the one deliberately carried along through the rewrite — comes out exactly the same as before. But the other kind, computed fresh from nothing but file and position, comes out as a completely different number.

That split exists on purpose. A freshly computed ID costs nothing to store, but it's only trustworthy within a single version — perfect for something like matching rows against themselves in one pass.
A materialized ID costs real storage to carry forward, but it's the only one that still means the same row after that row has physically moved.

Two more pieces round this out, named here rather than rebuilt. Low-shuffle merge is a real engine's own internal optimization — it keeps unmatched rows out of the expensive rewrite path entirely, which isn't something this sandbox has the machinery to reproduce.
And the outbound stream of everything MERGE just changed already has a home: that's Change Data Feed, built for real several topics back.
So: MERGE finds the files a condition touches, then rewrites them either completely or just where something actually changed.
A collision with a concurrent job gets caught and retried rather than silently lost, and a row keeps the identity that matters even after the file underneath it has changed.
